About

I help people understand new technology. The more complicated, the better.

I started my career in fintech and became a money person: how money moves, what it means to people, and what gets in the way. Like many families, mine had its share of money worries, so I want money to be easier to understand for everyone.

I’ll happily dig into how a payment rail works, then come back to the question that matters: “So what? Why should anyone care?”

Using a visual metaphor to explain ZBD’s role

How I developed “The Money Layer for Games” to explain ZBD’s role between games and financial services.

  • CompanyZBD
  • RoleSenior Product Marketing Manager

On this page

  1. Where money gets stuck
  2. From a barrier to a layer
  3. The line and the framework
  4. What I learned

TL;DR

Challenge
Explain ZBD’s role between game economies and financial systems.
Approach
Use a visual metaphor to understand the gap before naming it.
Output
“The Money Layer for Games” and the ZBD Platform messaging framework.

Where money gets stuck

In games, players can earn or buy items and currencies that have value within the game. Transferring that value to someone else or cashing it out can be difficult, so some trades happen through barter or off-platform arrangements. ZBD was building financial infrastructure to support money movement in games.

For a studio, adding these capabilities raises three issues:

  • Regulation: Handling player funds can trigger different requirements across markets, including licenses.
  • Game economy: Transfers and cash-out could change how an existing economy works.
  • Priorities: A new title or feature may offer a faster return than building financial infrastructure.

ZBD offered infrastructure that would be costly for studios to build themselves. I needed a clear way to explain its role.

From a barrier to a layer

Every draft that tried to carry both the problem and ZBD’s ambition picked up another clause. I stepped away from the copy and pictured an Eva pushing against an AT Field in Evangelion.

The AT Field was a layer that blocked passage between two spaces. Pushing harder would not get the Eva through, which made me think about the boundary itself. I pictured ZBD in a similar position between a game’s economy and the financial world, with infrastructure that could let value move across it.

The line and the framework

I used that image to develop “The Money Layer for Games.” The phrase described ZBD’s role across its products.

I shared the concept with leadership and the marketing team, then developed the ZBD Platform messaging framework around it.

The work also supported ZBD’s Series C fundraising, which closed in January 2026. “The Money Layer for Games” and the broader branding work contributed to how the company presented itself as it raised its next round.

What I learned

I had been trying to find the right words before I could see the relationship. Once I pictured the barrier and the layer that could bridge it, the line followed.

The Money Lifecycle

Explaining how ZBD’s products work together by following money into, through, and out of a game.

  • CompanyZBD
  • RoleSenior Product Marketing Manager
  • FollowsThe Money Layer for Games

On this page

  1. Players moved across STEP categories
  2. Following the money
  3. Money could stay in the game
  4. Used across messaging, decks, and the website
  5. What I learned

TL;DR

Challenge
STEP grouped ZBD’s products as Shop, Transfer, Earn, and Pay, but those categories overlapped as the platform grew.
Approach
Follow how value enters a game, moves within it, and leaves it. Use that flow to explain the products together.
Output
“Money In, Money Through, Money Out,” a lifecycle model now used in the ZBD Platform messaging framework, decks, and ZBD’s public website.

Players moved across STEP categories

After developing “The Money Layer for Games” to describe ZBD’s role, I needed a way to explain how the products beneath it worked together.

The existing framework was STEP: Shop, Transfer, Earn, and Pay. Its four categories were easy to remember, but a player’s experience rarely stayed inside one of them. Earn, now Embedded Rewards, made the overlap clear. A player could receive a reward, hold the value, spend it back in the game, send it to someone else, or cash out. Explaining that path meant moving across several STEP categories.

As ZBD’s portfolio expanded, I found myself spending more time explaining the boundaries than the products. I began looking for a model that followed the player’s experience instead.

Following the money

I started with two terms I knew from fintech: pay-in and payout. They described where money entered and left a system, but missed much of what ZBD could enable inside a game. Between those endpoints, players could earn, hold, spend, trade, and transfer value.

I tried calling the middle Pay Through, but “pay” made actions such as earning rewards and holding a balance sound like payments. “Money” covered those activities more naturally.

I settled on Money In, Money Through, Money Out. “Money Through” covered the activity within a game that STEP had spread across several categories.

Money could stay in the game

Once I drew the flow, a straight line felt incomplete. Value could enter a game, become a reward or a balance, move between players, and be spent within the game again. Some journeys ended in cash-out; others continued inside the economy.

I drew the three phases as a lifecycle to show how players could keep using value inside a game. A reward could become a balance, then a purchase or a transfer to another player.

Used across messaging, decks, and the website

I used the lifecycle in the ZBD Platform messaging framework and sales decks, and leadership began using the same language. We could explain the product suite without assigning each product to a single stage.

The same language appears on ZBD’s homepage, the Embedded Accounts page, and the August 2026 platform launch post. I also created the platform and product videos used across the site.

What I learned

Following a player’s money gave me a way to explain several products together. Each product could serve more than one stage, so the model still made sense as the portfolio grew.

Driving tech adoption (and how I changed customer behaviors)

Helping Korean American customers feel confident making their first digital money transfer.

  • CompanyWireBarley
  • RoleProduct Marketing Manager, first US marketing hire

On this page

  1. The most profitable audience had the lowest conversion rate
  2. Qualitative data revealed the need for a “hand-holding” experience
  3. What customers aged 50+ needed was reassurance
  4. Results
  5. What I learned

TL;DR

Challenge
Help Korean American customers aged 50+ complete their first transfer with WireBarley. Only about 20% of sign-ups in this group reached that point.
Approach
Use customer support call logs to understand where people needed reassurance, then show that support in a Korean-language TV commercial.
Result
In the period after the commercial aired, sign-up-to-first-transfer conversion in this group rose to nearly 50%.

The most profitable audience had the lowest conversion rate

As WireBarley’s first US marketing hire, I worked on bringing its digital remittance service to Korean American customers and adjacent Asian American communities. The service let people send money abroad without visiting a bank.

COVID lockdowns had accelerated the move toward contactless services, creating an opportunity for digital remittance. Earning people’s trust remained a challenge, especially when asking them to change how they handled money.

Internal data showed that customers aged 50+ were our most profitable audience, with average transfer amounts roughly $250 above the overall average. Yet many stopped early in identity verification, and only about 20% went on to make their first transfer. I wanted to understand what was holding them back.

Qualitative data revealed the need for a “hand-holding” experience

Before developing the commercial’s storyboard, I reviewed customer support call logs in Zendesk. Customers often mentioned that their sons or daughters would normally help them with this kind of task.

The conversations showed that these customers could take a photo of their ID, enter their information, and follow the verification steps. They needed someone they trusted to guide them while they learned an unfamiliar process.

WireBarley already had live customer support agents in the US who spoke Korean and English, alongside support in Thai, Mandarin, Vietnamese, Nepali, and other languages. I wanted the commercial to show how a Korean-speaking agent could help someone feel comfortable making their first transfer.

What customers aged 50+ needed was reassurance

I developed a TV commercial for local Korean-language channels serving Koreatowns across the US. TV was a familiar medium for this audience and complemented our existing newspaper and other mass-media advertising.

I wanted viewers to recognize their own situation and see how someone like them could complete a transfer with support. The commercial followed four steps:

Results

  • First-transfer conversion among customers aged 50+About 20% → nearly 50% after the commercial aired.
  • Broader business milestoneWireBarley led traditional Korean American banks in remittance volume to Korea during Chuseok, Korean Thanksgiving.
  • Media coverageFeatured on SBS America, representing the Korean American segment.

Other results at WireBarley

  • Led bilingual campaigns that drove $40M in holiday remittance volume. WireBarley reached the leading market position among Korean Americans by 2023.
  • Delivered 300% year-over-year US growth while operating within 40% of the previous year’s North American marketing budget.

What I learned

Finding the hesitation that prevents someone from acting can reveal a simple way to improve conversion. In fintech, showing customers that you understand their situation and have built an experience around their needs can give them a reason to trust you with their money.

A starter financial plan for people who aren’t money people

Answer a few questions about your paycheck, your bills, and what you’re saving for. You’ll leave with a budget, an emergency fund target, and a short list of what to do next.

  • TimeAbout 10 minutes
  • CostFree
  • Your answersStay in this browser

Your plan

I want money to feel less intimidating. This planner uses the rules of thumb most planners start with and shows the math behind each one. It’s for learning, so it never names a fund, a stock, or a brokerage.

Start with your paycheck

Everything in your plan is sized to the money that actually reaches your account.

Where to keep it

Keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account. The best ones pay more than 10 times the national average, and the money is still there when you need it.

  • Insured by the FDIC (banks) or NCUA (credit unions), up to $250,000
  • No monthly fee and no minimum balance to earn the rate
  • A rate that lasts, not a six-month promo
  • No direct deposit or monthly deposit requirement you can’t meet
  • Transfers to checking in one or two business days

What are you saving for?

    How do you feel about risk?

    Five quick questions about the money you won’t need for at least five years. There are no wrong answers.

    1When will you need most of your long-term money?
    2If you lost your income, how long could you cover bills without selling investments?
    3You invest $10,000. A month later it’s worth $7,000. What do you do?
    4Which would you pick for one year?
    5Have you invested before?
    Step 5 of 8

    Find the free money first

    If your employer matches what you put into a retirement plan, that match is usually the best return you can get.

    Does your job offer a retirement plan?

    A 401(k), 403(b), 457(b), TSP, or SIMPLE IRA all count.

    How does your employer match?

    Check your benefits site or ask HR for the plan summary.

    Enter it as a share of your pay, like 3 for 3%.

    %
    When is the match fully yours?

    Your own contributions are always yours. The match can take time.

    Does the plan offer a Roth 401(k)?
    Are you on a high-deductible health plan with an HSA?
    Step 6 of 8

    Decide how much to invest

    A common target is 15% of your pay before taxes for retirement, counting your employer’s match.

    Ways to invest

    Once you know how much, you pick how. These are the main options, from least effort to most.

    Target-date funds

    One fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds and gets more careful as its target year gets closer. It’s the default in many 401(k) plans.

    Lowest effort. Check the yearly fee, called the expense ratio, since it varies a lot.

    Index funds and ETFs

    One fund holds hundreds or thousands of companies by tracking a market index, so no single company can sink you.

    Low effort, wide spread, and yearly fees that are often under 0.10%.

    Robo-advisors

    An app asks about your goals, builds a portfolio of funds, and rebalances it for you.

    Low effort outside a 401(k). Expect a fee of about 0.25% a year on top of the funds’ own fees.

    Individual stocks

    You buy shares of one company at a time. It’s a good way to learn and a risky way to save.

    High effort and little spread unless you own many. Many people keep this to a small slice, under 10%.

    Why fees matter

    A 1% yearly fee sounds small. On $500 a month for 30 years at a 6% return, you’d end up with about $80,000 less than with a 0.05% fee.

    Investing on autopilot

    Putting the same amount in every payday, through ups and downs, means you buy more when prices drop. It also takes the guessing out.

    Rebalancing

    Once a year, move money back to your target mix. If stocks had a great year, that means trimming them.

    Step 7 of 8

    Here’s your plan

    These are your next moves, in order. Do the first one this week.
